title: Milk and blood
hook: tradition says he squeezed Lalo's bread and milk ran out, and from Bhago's feast, blood

segments.voice: Yesterday: kirat, honest work, and Lalo's coarse bread chosen over a rich man's feast.

A tense room in Saidpur. Malik Bhago, the rich official, has summoned Guru Nanak to explain himself: why eat a carpenter's coarse bread and snub my feast? The townspeople crowd in. Everyone wants to see what happens when a holy man with nothing insults a man with everything. And here, as tradition tells it, the dinner-party drama becomes something stranger. Nanak asks for two things: a piece of Lalo's bread, and a piece of food from Bhago's table. He takes one in each hand.
screen: `A TENSE ROOM IN SAIDPUR.` → `ONE PIECE FROM EACH TABLE.` → `ONE IN EACH HAND.`

segments.voice: Tradition says he pressed them. From Lalo's bread, milk ran out. From Bhago's rich food, blood. That's the whole scene, told in gurdwaras and children's books and painted on walls. Sikhs read it in more than one way. Some take it as a miracle that really happened, a sign given to a proud man. Others read it as a picture, a parable in the language of the janamsakhis, which are full of wonders. Plainly put, the milk and the blood aren't in the scripture itself; they come from the later life stories. What the scripture has is the idea underneath, in Guru Nanak's own words. In one hymn, he says that taking what rightfully belongs to another is as forbidden as pork is to a Muslim and beef is to a Hindu. He reaches for the one thing each of his neighbors would never eat, and says: that's what stolen wealth is. So in either reading, the point is the same. Food carries its history. Lalo's bread came from sweat, and it nourishes, like milk. Bhago's feast came from taxes and bribes and squeezing people who had little, so in the story's startling picture, it's made of their blood. Nobody could see it on the plate. The story makes it visible, and asks a question that doesn't expire: not how much, or how nice, but how was it earned? Tradition says Bhago was shaken, and changed his ways.
screen: `FROM LALO'S BREAD, MILK.` · `FROM BHAGO'S FEAST, BLOOD.` · `MIRACLE OR PARABLE: SIKHS READ BOTH.` · `FOOD CARRIES ITS HISTORY.` · then, large: `HOW WAS IT EARNED?`

segments.voice: Pick one thing near you, your shoes, your phone, the chair, and trace it back as far as you can: who made it, where, who carried it, who was paid, and who maybe wasn't. You won't know all of it, and that's fine. Follow it as far as it goes, without guilt and without a verdict.
Hakk. What rightfully belongs to another, the idea behind the milk and blood tradition says ran from Lalo's honest bread and Bhago's stolen feast.
Your line: how was it earned. Tomorrow, a rest house on the road. That's thirty-four days.

howItsDone: Sikhs tell the milk-and-blood sakhi as a teaching about honest earnings; many gurdwaras and families use it to explain why kirat, honest work, matters, and some Sikhs give a tenth of their income, dasvandh, from earnings made honestly.

original.note: Gurmukhi: hakk, what rightfully belongs to someone, from Arabic haqq; the word in Nanak's line about another's due.

trapdoor: what you thought: a magic trick with bread.
what it means: food carries its history. honest bread nourishes like milk; wealth squeezed from the poor is, in the story's picture, their blood.
what a scholar hears: a janamsakhi wonder, not in the scripture, built on a real hymn that likens taking another's due to pork for a Muslim and beef for a Hindu.

notes: The salok 'hakk paraaiaa naanakaa us sooar us gaai' is placed in Var Majh at Ang 141; confirm Ang and paraphrase.
The milk-and-blood episode is absent from some early janamsakhis and prominent in later tradition; the script says only that it comes from 'the later life stories' and not the scripture. Confirm.
Two readings (literal miracle, parable) presented without ranking; confirm acceptable.
